notes.front: What does 'grounded' mean in Subpart K?
notes.back: Connected to earth or to some conducting body that serves in place of the earth.
notes.explanation: Earth itself is not required: a conducting body standing in for the earth also counts.
notes.example: Like a metal site cabin frame wired back to an earth electrode, as opposed to one resting on rubber blocks with no connection at all.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.449, p. 245
notes.evidence: Grounded. Connected to earth or to some conducting body that serves in place of the earth.

notes.front: What is a ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI)?
notes.back: A personnel-protection device that de-energises a circuit within a set time when current to ground exceeds a value below the overcurrent device's operating level.
notes.explanation: It is defined as protection for personnel, and it acts on a current to ground smaller than the one that would operate the supply circuit's overcurrent protective device.
notes.example: Like the socket with test and reset buttons on a bathroom circuit at home, but here fitted to the temporary power that site workers plug into.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.449, p. 246
notes.evidence: A device for the protection of personnel that functions to deenergize a circuit or portion thereof within an established period of time when a current to ground exceeds some predetermined value that is less than that required to operate the overcurrent protective device of the supply circuit.

notes.front: What is an assured equipment grounding conductor program (AEGCP)?
notes.back: A program the employer sets up and runs on site, covering cord sets, receptacles not part of the building, and cord-and-plug equipment employees use.
notes.explanation: The program must meet stated minimum requirements, starting with a written description of it.
notes.example: Like a hire firm's log of every lead and plug-in tool it checks and tests, kept on the site where those leads and tools are used.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii), p. 224
notes.evidence: establish and implement an assured equipment grounding conductor program on construction sites covering all cord sets, receptacles which are not a part of the building or structure, and equipment connected by cord and plug which are available for use or used by employees. This program shall comply with the following minimum requirements: (A) A written description of the program

notes.front: Besides hazards from using electricity at jobsites, what do the Subpart K safety-related work practices also cover?
notes.back: Accidental contact, direct or indirect, with any energised lines, above or below ground, passing through or near the jobsite.
notes.explanation: Those work practices sit in §§ 1926.416 and 1926.417, and their reach extends to lines that merely pass through or near the site.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.400(b), p. 220
notes.evidence: Safety-related work practices are contained in §§ 1926.416 and 1926.417. In addition to covering the hazards arising from the use of electricity at jobsites, these regulations also cover the hazards arising from the accidental contact, direct or indirect, by employees with all energized lines, above or below ground, passing through or near the jobsite.

notes.front: A crew digs beside a live buried cable that crosses the site but supplies a neighbouring building, not the project. Do the Subpart K work practices cover the risk of contact with it?
notes.choices:
A) Yes: they cover energised lines above or below ground passing through or near the jobsite
B) No: only lines supplying the project are covered
C) No: only overhead lines are covered
D) Only if the crew is using electric tools
notes.back: A: yes; they cover energised lines above or below ground passing through or near the jobsite.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule does not ask whom a line supplies. C: lines below ground are named expressly. D: contact with lines is covered in addition to hazards from using electricity.
notes.explanation: The cable is energised, below ground and passing through the jobsite, which puts accidental contact with it within scope.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.400(b), p. 220
notes.evidence: In addition to covering the hazards arising from the use of electricity at jobsites, these regulations also cover the hazards arising from the accidental contact, direct or indirect, by employees with all energized lines, above or below ground, passing through or near the jobsite.

notes.front: What two ways does Subpart K give an employer to protect employees from ground faults on a construction site?
notes.back: Ground-fault circuit interrupters, or an assured equipment grounding conductor program.
notes.explanation: Either route comes on top of any other requirements for equipment grounding conductors; it does not replace them.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(i), p. 224
notes.evidence: The employer shall use either ground fault circuit interrupters as specified in paragraph (b)(1)(ii) of this section or an assured equipment grounding conductor program as specified in paragraph (b)(1)(iii) of this section to protect employees on construction sites. These requirements are in addition to any other requirements for equipment grounding conductors.

notes.front: Under the GFCI option, all {{c1::120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere}} receptacle outlets on construction sites that are not part of the permanent wiring and are in use by employees must have approved GFCIs.
notes.explanation: The rule targets temporary outlets: receptacles that are part of the building's permanent wiring fall outside it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(ii), p. 224
notes.evidence: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20ampere receptacle outlets on construction sites, which are not a part of the permanent wiring of the building or structure and which are in use by employees, shall have approved groundfault circuit interrupters for personnel protection.

notes.front: Which generator receptacles need no GFCI protection?
notes.back: Those on a two-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generator of up to 5 kW, its conductors insulated from the frame and grounded surfaces.
notes.explanation: Every condition must hold together: the size limit, the two-wire single-phase design and the insulation of the circuit conductors.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(ii), p. 224
notes.evidence: Receptacles on a two-wire, single-phase portable or vehiclemounted generator rated not more than 5kW, where the circuit conductors of the generator are insulated from the generator frame and all other grounded surfaces, need not be protected with ground-fault circuit interrupters.

notes.front: Joiners plug saws into a 120-volt, single-phase, 20-ampere outlet on a temporary distribution box fed from the site supply. The employer runs no assured equipment grounding conductor program. What must the outlet have?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the saws are double-insulated
B) A warning label
C) A 30-ampere fuse
D) An approved GFCI
notes.back: D: an approved GFCI.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duty attaches to the outlet, whatever tool is plugged in. B: a label is not ground-fault protection. C: a larger fuse is overcurrent protection, not the personnel protection the rule requires.
notes.explanation: With no assured program, the employer must use the GFCI route, and this is a temporary 120-volt, 20-ampere outlet in use by employees.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(ii), p. 224
notes.evidence: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20ampere receptacle outlets on construction sites, which are not a part of the permanent wiring of the building or structure and which are in use by employees, shall have approved groundfault circuit interrupters for personnel protection.

notes.front: Where must the written description of an AEGCP be kept, and for whom?
notes.back: At the jobsite, available for inspection and copying by the Assistant Secretary and any affected employee.
notes.explanation: The description must set out the specific procedures the employer has adopted, not just state that a program exists.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(A), p. 224
notes.evidence: A written description of the program, including the specific procedures adopted by the employer, shall be available at the jobsite for inspection and copying by the Assistant Secretary and any affected employee.

notes.front: The employer must designate one or more {{c1::competent persons}} to implement the assured equipment grounding conductor program.
notes.explanation: The rule points back to the general definition of a competent person in § 1926.32(f).
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(B), p. 224
notes.evidence: The employer shall designate one or more competent persons (as defined in § 1926.32(f)) to implement the program.

notes.front: Under an AEGCP, when must cord sets, plugs, receptacles and cord-and-plug equipment be visually inspected?
notes.back: Before each day's use, for external defects and signs of possible internal damage, unless fixed and not exposed to damage.
notes.explanation: Deformed or missing pins and damaged insulation are examples, and equipment found damaged must not be used until repaired.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(C), p. 224
notes.evidence: except cord sets and receptacles which are fixed and not exposed to damage, shall be visually inspected before each day’s use for external defects, such as deformed or missing pins or insulation damage, and for indications of possible internal damage. Equipment found damaged or defective shall not be used until repaired.

notes.front: Which two tests does an AEGCP require on cord sets, non-permanent receptacles and cord-and-plug equipment that must be grounded?
notes.back: A continuity test of all equipment grounding conductors, and a test that the equipment grounding conductor is correctly attached at each receptacle and plug.
notes.explanation: The conductors must prove electrically continuous, and the equipment grounding conductor must sit on its proper terminal.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(D), p. 224
notes.evidence: (1) All equipment grounding conductors shall be tested for continuity and shall be electrically continuous. (2) Each receptacle and attachment cap or plug shall be tested for correct attachment of the equipment grounding conductor. The equipment grounding conductor shall be connected to its proper terminal.

notes.front: Besides before first use, after repairs and after suspected damage, AEGCP tests must be done at intervals not exceeding {{c1::3 months}}.
notes.explanation: Cord sets and receptacles that are fixed and not exposed to damage may go up to 6 months between tests.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E), pp. 224–225
notes.evidence: (4) At intervals not to exceed 3 months, except that cord sets and receptacles which are fixed and not exposed to damage shall be tested at intervals not exceeding 6 months.

notes.front: Under an AEGCP, a cord set last tested six weeks ago is caught under a falling pallet of blocks this morning. When must it next be tested?
notes.choices:
A) Before it is used again
B) At the next 3-month interval
C) Within 6 months
D) Only if it later fails to work
notes.back: A: before it is used again.
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are routine intervals, which do not wait once damage is suspected. D: the rule turns on suspected damage, not on a failure showing.
notes.explanation: An incident that can reasonably be suspected of damaging the equipment triggers a test before it is used again.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E), p. 225
notes.evidence: (3) Before equipment is used after any incident which can be reasonably suspected to have caused damage

notes.front: Extension cord sets used with portable electric tools and appliances must be of {{c1::three-wire}} type and designed for hard or extra-hard usage.
notes.explanation: Flexible cords for temporary and portable lights must also be designed for hard or extra-hard usage.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(J), p. 231
notes.evidence: Extension cord sets used with portable electric tools and appliances shall be of three-wire type and shall be designed for hard or extra-hard usage. Flexible cords used with temporary and portable lights shall be designed for hard or extra-hard usage.

notes.front: A supervisor brings a light two-wire extension lead from home to run a hammer drill on site. What does Subpart K require of an extension cord set used this way?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as the lead is short
B) Only that it be a bright colour
C) Only that it be plugged into a fused outlet
D) That it be three-wire type and designed for hard or extra-hard usage
notes.back: D: three-wire type, designed for hard or extra-hard usage.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule sets no length exception. B: colour is not a requirement of this rule. C: fusing the outlet does not change what the cord itself must be.
notes.explanation: A hammer drill is a portable electric tool, so its extension cord set falls under the three-wire, hard-usage rule; a two-wire lead fails it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(J), p. 231
notes.evidence: Extension cord sets used with portable electric tools and appliances shall be of three-wire type and shall be designed for hard or extra-hard usage.

notes.front: May a flexible cord pass through a doorway or other pinch point?
notes.back: Yes, if protection is provided to avoid damage to it.
notes.explanation: The general rule is that flexible cords and cables be protected from damage, with sharp corners and projections avoided.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(I), p. 231
notes.evidence: (I) Flexible cords and cables shall be protected from damage. Sharp corners and projections shall be avoided. Flexible cords and cables may pass through doorways or other pinch points, if protection is provided to avoid damage.

notes.front: {{c1::Worn or frayed}} electric cords or cables must not be used.
notes.explanation: The same paragraph bars fastening extension cords with staples, hanging them from nails or suspending them by wire.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(e), p. 240
notes.evidence: (e) Cords and cables. (1) Worn or frayed electric cords or cables shall not be used. (2) Extension cords shall not be fastened with staples, hung from nails, or suspended by wire.

notes.front: Before a shift, a joiner sees that the sheath of his extension lead is frayed near the plug. May he use it for one quick cut?
notes.back: No. Worn or frayed electric cords must not be used, however short the job.
notes.explanation: The rule has no exception for brief use, so the length of the task makes no difference.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(e)(1), p. 240
notes.evidence: (1) Worn or frayed electric cords or cables shall not be used.

notes.front: The path to ground from circuits, equipment and enclosures must be {{c1::permanent and continuous}}.
notes.explanation: The next paragraph requires metal cable trays, metal raceways and metal enclosures for conductors to be grounded, with limited exceptions.
notes.evidence: (6) Grounding path. The path to ground from circuits, equipment, and enclosures shall be permanent and continuous. (7) Supports, enclosures, and equipment to be grounded—(i) Supports and enclosures for conductors. Metal cable trays, metal raceways, and metal enclosures for conductors shall be grounded, except that:

notes.front: Which grounding arrangement for a site distribution board meets the grounding-path rule?
notes.choices:
A) A ground connection made only while tools are running
B) A ground connection that breaks whenever the board's door is opened
C) A ground lead clipped on only during inspections
D) A permanent and continuous path to ground
notes.back: D: a permanent and continuous path to ground.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are temporary, so the path is not permanent. B is interrupted each time the door opens, so the path is not continuous.
notes.explanation: The rule asks for both qualities at once: the path must be permanent and it must be continuous.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.404(f)(6), p. 228
notes.evidence: The path to ground from circuits, equipment, and enclosures shall be permanent and continuous.

notes.front: What must electric power-operated tools be, under § 1926.302(a)?
notes.back: Either of the approved double-insulated type, or grounded in line with Subpart K.
notes.explanation: The same paragraph forbids using a tool's electric cord to hoist or lower it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.302(a), p. 204
notes.evidence: (1) Electric power operated tools shall either be of the approved double-insulated type or grounded in accordance with subpart K of this part. (2) The use of electric cords for hoisting or lowering tools shall not be permitted.

notes.front: Live parts of electric equipment operating at {{c1::50 volts}} or more must be guarded against accidental contact.
notes.explanation: Guarding may be by cabinets or other enclosures, or by location, such as a room or vault accessible only to qualified persons.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.403(i)(2)(i), p. 222
notes.evidence: live parts of electric equipment operating at 50 volts or more shall be guarded against accidental contact by cabinets or other forms of enclosures, or by any of the following means: (A) By location in a room, vault, or similar enclosure that is accessible only to qualified persons.

notes.front: A temporary panel with exposed live parts at 120 volts stands in an open corridor that every trade uses. What does Subpart K require?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because 120 volts is below the guarding threshold
B) Guarding against accidental contact, for example by an enclosure
C) A warning sign only
D) Guarding only if the panel exceeds 600 volts
notes.back: B: guarding against accidental contact, for example by an enclosure.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D put the threshold too high: it is 50 volts. C: a sign is not one of the guarding means the rule lists.
notes.explanation: 120 volts is above the 50-volt threshold, and a corridor open to all trades is not limited to qualified persons.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.403(i)(2)(i), p. 222
notes.evidence: live parts of electric equipment operating at 50 volts or more shall be guarded against accidental contact by cabinets or other forms of enclosures, or by any of the following means: (A) By location in a room, vault, or similar enclosure that is accessible only to qualified persons.

notes.front: How high above the floor must live parts be to count as guarded by elevation?
notes.back: 8 feet (2.44 m) or more above the floor or other working surface, installed so as to exclude unqualified persons.
notes.explanation: A balcony, gallery or platform can serve the same purpose when it is elevated and arranged to keep unqualified persons out.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.403(i)(2)(i)(C)–(D), p. 222
notes.evidence: (C) By location on a balcony, gallery, or platform so elevated and arranged as to exclude unqualified persons. (D) By elevation of 8 feet (2.44 m) or more above the floor or other working surface and so installed as to exclude unqualified persons.

notes.front: When may an employer let an employee work close enough to an electric power circuit to contact it?
notes.back: Only when the employee is protected against shock by de-energising and grounding the circuit, or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means.
notes.explanation: The duty is framed as a ban on the employer: no such work is permitted without one of those protections.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(1), p. 240
notes.evidence: No employer shall permit an employee to work in such proximity to any part of an electric power circuit that the employee could contact the electric power circuit in the course of work, unless the employee is protected against electric shock by deenergizing the circuit and grounding it or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means.

notes.front: A crew must fix brackets within arm's reach of a live 480-volt busway, close enough to touch it. Which approach does § 1926.416 accept?
notes.choices:
A) Carry on, using the most experienced worker
B) Carry on, provided everyone wears hard hats
C) De-energise and ground the busway, or guard it effectively by insulation
D) Post a warning sign and carry on
notes.back: C: de-energise and ground it, or guard it effectively by insulation.
notes.choicesExplained: A: experience is not one of the protections the rule names. B: hard hats do not protect against contact with the circuit. D: a sign does not de-energise or guard the circuit.
notes.explanation: The workers could contact the circuit, so the rule requires one of its two protections before work goes ahead.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(1), p. 240
notes.evidence: unless the employee is protected against electric shock by deenergizing the circuit and grounding it or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means.

notes.front: Before work begins, how must the employer find out whether the work could bring anyone into contact with an energised power circuit?
notes.back: By inquiry, direct observation or instruments.
notes.explanation: The check covers exposed and concealed circuits, and contact by any person, tool or machine.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(3), p. 240
notes.evidence: Before work is begun the employer shall ascertain by inquiry or direct observation, or by instruments, whether any part of an energized electric power circuit, exposed or concealed, is so located that the performance of the work may bring any person, tool, or machine into physical or electrical contact with the electric power circuit.

notes.front: Where such a circuit exists, what must the employer do besides locating it?
notes.back: Post and maintain proper warning signs, and advise employees of the lines' location, the hazards and the protective measures to take.
notes.explanation: Finding the circuit is only the first step: the employees doing the work must also be told where it is and how they are to be protected.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(3), p. 240
notes.evidence: The employer shall post and maintain proper warning signs where such a circuit exists. The employer shall advise employees of the location of such lines, the hazards involved, and the protective measures to be taken.

notes.front: Where the exact location of underground power lines is unknown, what must employees using jack-hammers or bars be given?
notes.back: Insulated protective gloves.
notes.explanation: The requirement reaches any hand tool that may contact a line, not only jack-hammers and bars.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(2), p. 240
notes.evidence: In work areas where the exact location of underground electric powerlines is unknown, employees using jack-hammers, bars, or other hand tools which may contact a line shall be provided with insulated protective gloves.

notes.front: A contractor will break out a ground-floor slab. The drawings do not show whether a power cable runs beneath it. What must the employer do before work begins?
notes.choices:
A) Rely on the drawings, since they show no cable
B) Start work and stop if a cable appears
C) Find out, by inquiry, direct observation or instruments, whether an energised circuit could be contacted
D) Ask workers to report any cable they hit
notes.back: C: find out by inquiry, direct observation or instruments whether an energised circuit could be contacted.
notes.choicesExplained: B and D find the cable only by reaching it, after work has begun. A: drawings that are silent do not settle whether a concealed circuit is there.
notes.explanation: The duty to ascertain applies before work is begun and covers concealed circuits as well as exposed ones.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.416(a)(3), p. 240
notes.evidence: Before work is begun the employer shall ascertain by inquiry or direct observation, or by instruments, whether any part of an energized electric power circuit, exposed or concealed, is so located that the performance of the work may bring any person, tool, or machine into physical or electrical contact with the electric power circuit.

notes.front: Under § 1926.417, what must be done to equipment or circuits that are de-energised?
notes.back: Render them inoperative and attach tags at all points where they can be energised.
notes.explanation: The tags must be placed so that they plainly identify the equipment or circuits being worked on.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.417(b)–(c), p. 240
notes.evidence: Equipment or circuits that are deenergized shall be rendered inoperative and shall have tags attached at all points where such equipment or circuits can be energized. (c) Tags. Tags shall be placed to identify plainly the equipment or circuits being worked on.

notes.front: Controls that are to be deactivated during work on energised or de-energised equipment or circuits must be {{c1::tagged}}.
notes.explanation: The rule applies whichever state the equipment is in, and the next rule adds tags at every point where de-energised equipment could be energised.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.417(a)–(b), p. 240
notes.evidence: (a) Controls. Controls that are to be deactivated during the course of work on energized or deenergized equipment or circuits shall be tagged. (b) Equipment and circuits. Equipment or circuits that are deenergized shall be rendered inoperative and shall have tags attached at all points where such equipment or circuits can be energized.

notes.front: An electrician de-energises a feeder that can be energised from two panels. She makes the nearer panel inoperative and tags it, but does nothing at the other. What is missing?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: one tag is enough
B) A second electrician to watch
C) Making the feeder inoperative and tagging it at the other panel too
D) A GFCI on the feeder
notes.back: C: making it inoperative and tagging it at the other panel too.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule asks for tags at all points of energising, not one. B: a watcher is not what the rule requires. D: a GFCI is ground-fault protection, not tagging of de-energised circuits.
notes.explanation: The other panel is also a point where the feeder can be energised, so it needs the same treatment.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.417(b), p. 240
notes.evidence: Equipment or circuits that are deenergized shall be rendered inoperative and shall have tags attached at all points where such equipment or circuits can be energized.

notes.front: In crane and derrick work, when may the employer treat a power line as not energised?
notes.back: Only when the utility owner/operator confirms it has been and continues to be de-energised and visibly grounded at the worksite.
notes.explanation: The default runs the other way: the employer must assume that all power lines are energised.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1408(e), p. 682
notes.evidence: The employer must assume that all power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.

notes.front: A utility tells a crane contractor that a nearby line 'should be off today', but does not confirm that it is de-energised and visibly grounded at the worksite. How must the employer treat the line?
notes.choices:
A) As de-energised, because the utility said so
B) As energised
C) As de-energised for lifts that stay low
D) As de-energised if no arcing is seen
notes.back: B: as energised.
notes.choicesExplained: A: 'should be off' is not a confirmation that it has been and continues to be de-energised and visibly grounded. D and C rest on the crew's own judgement, which the rule does not accept in place of the utility's confirmation.
notes.explanation: Without the utility owner/operator's confirmation, the rule's default applies: all power lines are assumed energised.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1407(f), p. 680
notes.evidence: The employer must assume that all power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.

notes.front: Before crane operations near a power line of up to 350 kV, what finding obliges the employer to follow Option (1), (2) or (3) of § 1926.1408?
notes.back: That any part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than 20 feet to a power line, up to maximum working radius.
notes.explanation: Option (1) is the utility's confirmation that the line is de-energised and visibly grounded; Option (2) is keeping a 20-foot clearance.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1408(a)(2), p. 681
notes.evidence: could get closer than 20 feet to a power line. If so, the employer must meet the requirements in Option (1), Option (2), or Option (3) of this section, as follows: (i) Option (1)—Deenergize and ground. Confirm from the utility owner/operator that the power line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite. (ii) Option (2)—20 foot clearance.

notes.front: In Table A of § 1926.1408, the minimum clearance distance for a power line of up to 50 kV is {{c1::10 feet}}.
notes.explanation: The distances rise with voltage, through 15, 20, 25 and 35 feet to 45 feet for lines over 750 up to 1,000 kV.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1408, Table A, p. 683
notes.evidence: 10 15 20 25 35 45 (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution).

notes.front: In Table A, who establishes the minimum clearance distance for power lines over 1,000 kV?
notes.back: The utility owner/operator, or a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person in power transmission and distribution.
notes.explanation: Table A gives no fixed figure above 1,000 kV; its fixed distances stop at 45 feet for the band up to 1,000 kV.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1408, Table A, p. 683
notes.evidence: 10 15 20 25 35 45 (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution).

notes.front: A mobile crane will work near a 350 kV line under Option (3). Which Table A band, and minimum clearance distance, applies?
notes.choices:
A) Over 350 to 500 kV: 25 feet
B) Over 50 to 200 kV: 15 feet
C) Up to 50 kV: 10 feet
D) Over 200 to 350 kV: 20 feet
notes.back: D: over 200 to 350 kV, with 20 feet.
notes.choicesExplained: A: 'over 350' starts above 350 kV, so a 350 kV line is not in that band. C and B are bands for lower voltages.
notes.explanation: Table A's note says the value after 'to' is included, so 'over 200 to 350' runs up to and including 350 kV.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1408, Table A and note, p. 683
notes.evidence: Note: The value that follows ‘‘to’’ is up to and includes that value. For example, over 50 to 200 means up to and including 200kV.
